content: An antiemetic is a medication designed to prevent or alleviate nausea and vomiting. These drugs are commonly used to manage symptoms associated with motion sickness, side effects of opioid analgesics, general anesthetics, and chemotherapy for cancer treatment. Types of Antiemetics 1. 5-HT3 Receptor Antagonists These drugs block serotonin receptors in the central nervous system and gastrointestinal tract. They are particularly effective in treating nausea and vomiting caused by postoperative conditions or cytotoxic drugs. Examples include: Dolasetron Granisetron Ondansetron Tropisetron Palonosetron (Aloxi, a newer 5-HT3 antagonist) 2. Dopamine Antagonists Dopamine antagonists act on the brain to manage nausea and vomiting associated with neoplastic diseases, radiation sickness, opioids, cytotoxic drugs, and general anesthetics. Examples include: Domperidone Droperidol Haloperidol Chlorpromazine Promethazine Prochlorperazine Some of these drugs are limited in their use due to side effects such as extrapyramidal symptoms and sedation. Metoclopramide, which also acts as a prokinetic agent in the gastrointestinal tract, is useful for gastrointestinal diseases but less effective for cytotoxic or postoperative vomiting. Alizapride is another example. 3. Antihistamines (H1 Receptor Antagonists) These are effective in treating conditions such as motion sickness and severe morning sickness during pregnancy. Examples include: Cyclizine Diphenhydramine Dimenhydrinate Meclizine Promethazine (marketed as Pentazine, Phenergan, or Promacot) Hydroxyzine 4. Cannabinoids Cannabinoids are used in patients with cachexia, cytotoxic-induced nausea and vomiting, or those unresponsive to other treatments. Examples include: Cannabis (Marijuana): Many patients prefer smoked or vaporized cannabis over pharmaceutical versions because it contains all 66 cannabinoids, many of which have medicinal properties. Dronabinol (Marinol): Primarily used by cancer and AIDS patients, with some use for pain, multiple sclerosis, and Alzheimer’s disease. Nabilone (Cesamet): Reintroduced to the market in late 2006, it is classified as a Schedule II substance, unlike Marinol (Schedule III) and cannabis (Schedule I). Sativex: An oral spray containing THC and CBD. 5. Benzodiazepines Midazolam: When administered at the onset of anesthesia, it has been shown in recent trials to be as effective as ondansetron (a 5-HT3 antagonist) in preventing postoperative nausea and vomiting. Further studies are needed. Lorazepam: Often used as an adjunct treatment for nausea alongside first-line medications like Compazine or Zofran. 6. Anticholinergics Hyoscine (Scopolamine): Commonly used for motion sickness. 7. Steroids Dexamethasone: Administered in low doses at the onset of general anesthesia for surgery, it is an effective antiemetic. The exact mechanism of action remains unclear. 8. Other Agents Trimethobenzamide: Thought to act on the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ). Ginger: Claimed to be effective in reducing nausea. Emetrol: Marketed as an antiemetic. Propofol: Administered intravenously, it has been used in acute care settings as a rescue therapy for severe emesis. Peppermint: Claimed to alleviate nausea or stomach pain when consumed as tea or candies. Muscimol: Purported to have antiemetic properties. Non-Pharmaceutical Therapies Acupuncture and hypnosis have shown some evidence of efficacy in managing nausea and vomiting. Important Considerations All antiemetic drugs have potential side effects. It is crucial to minimize the baseline risk of nausea and vomiting, particularly in surgical settings, to optimize patient outcomes.
